title: Java String — characters, indexing and the costs that bite
summary: Strings are immutable, char arithmetic, building with StringBuilder, substring cost and index convention, and conversions.
note:
1. Basics
   • `String` is **immutable**: read with `s.charAt(i)`, `s.length()`; build with `StringBuilder`
   • Characters are numbers: `'a'`=97, `'A'`=65, `'0'`=48
   • `c - 'a'` → 0..25 · `c - '0'` → 0..9
2. Helpers
   • `Character.toLowerCase/toUpperCase/isLetter/isDigit/isLetterOrDigit/isWhitespace`
   • Ignore case → lowercase everything before comparing (`s.equalsIgnoreCase(t)` for whole strings)
3. Building strings
   • `StringBuilder sb; sb.append(c);` then `sb.toString()` → O(1) amortised per append
   • `s = s + c` in a loop → O(n) each time → O(n²) ✗
   • Build then `sb.reverse()` instead of inserting at the front
4. Costs
   • `substring(i, j)` → O(j − i), end-exclusive · `a.equals(b)` → O(length) · hashing a String → O(length) (cached)
5. Conversions
   • `Integer.toString(123)` / `String.valueOf(123)`, `Integer.parseInt("123")`, `Long.parseLong`, `"x".repeat(n)`
✎ In my words: ______________________________________________

recall.q: Why avoid `s = s + c` in a loop?
recall.a: String is immutable, so each concat copies the whole string → O(n²). Use a StringBuilder.

recall.q: What does `s.substring(i, j)` take as its second argument?
recall.a: An end index that is exclusive (not a length, unlike C++'s substr) — it returns chars [i, j).

recall.q: How do you compare two strings ignoring case?
recall.a: `a.equalsIgnoreCase(b)`, or lowercase each char with `Character.toLowerCase` before comparing.

for (char c : s.toCharArray()) cnt[c - 'a']++;   // letter frequency
int d = ch - '0';                                 // digit value
boolean ok = Character.isLetterOrDigit(c);        // letter or digit

sections.title: Basics
Building strings efficiently
sections.body:
✍️ Use a `StringBuilder`: `sb.append(c);` is amortised O(1). Call `sb.toString()` once at the end.
✍️ `s = s + c;` builds a brand-new String each time because String is immutable → O(length) → O(n²) in a loop. Never concatenate in a loop.
✍️ Build forwards then `sb.reverse()` rather than inserting at the front (`sb.insert(0, …)` is O(n)).

sections.title: substring and comparisons
sections.body:
✍️ `s.substring(i, j)` returns the chars at [i, j) — the second argument is an **end index, not a length** (the opposite of C++'s `substr(pos, len)`). It allocates a new String → O(j − i). Calling it inside a loop over all positions is O(n²) or worse.
✍️ Compare with `a.equals(b)` (O(min length)); never use `==`, which compares references. A String's `hashCode()` is computed once and cached, so repeated map lookups don't re-hash.
- `s.indexOf(t)` is O(n·m) in the worst case — fine for small inputs, not for 10⁵.

sections.title: Conversions
sections.body:
- `String.valueOf(123)` / `Integer.toString(123)` → `"123"`; `Integer.parseInt("123")` → 123; `Long.parseLong` for long.
- `"x".repeat(n)` → n copies of "x"; `new String(charArray)` from a `char[]`.
- `s.split("\\s+")` splits on whitespace, or stream tokens via `new Scanner(s)` (see [[str-tokenising-and-reversal]]).

sections.title: Pitfalls
sections.body:
✍️ `char` arithmetic on uppercase vs lowercase: `'A' - 'a'` is negative. Normalise with `Character.toLowerCase` first when the problem ignores case.
- `Character.isLetter`/`toLowerCase` have `int` (code-point) overloads; for the full Unicode range iterate with `codePointAt`, but LeetCode inputs are ASCII, so the `char` versions are fine.
